turns.content:
Hey, can I run something by you? Last night at dinner my partner Leo kept using 'they' for my brother Julian, who's a trans man and uses he/him. Three times. Julian went quiet and left early. I drafted a text this morning but I'm second-guessing the tone.

~EDIT: I wrote: "Hey, last night at dinner you used 'they' for Julian three times. He's a man. Please just use he/him. I know you mean well but it matters."

Is that too sharp? Or is texting the next day itself a bad move? I just want an honest read — not a rewrite, just whether my irritation is leaking.

Your irritation isn't really leaking — the text is direct but kind. Here's my honest read:

**The text works.** It states a fact (three times), states the need (he/him), and the last line gives Leo credit while explaining why it matters. That's about as clean as a correction gets. If anything, "I know you mean well" is the only line that could be read as slightly pointed, but it's also genuinely generous and probably true, so I'd leave it.

**Texting the next day is fine — arguably better than in the moment.** Correcting someone mid-dinner in front of Julian can feel like calling attention to him, which is often worse for the person being misgendered. A private message the next day lets Leo absorb it without an audience. The only thing texting can't do is convey tone of voice, but your draft's tone is calm enough that it survives text.

One thing worth sitting with: your irritation is present, but it's proportionate. Julian went quiet and left early — you're not escalating, you're addressing something that actually hurt someone. A slightly sharp edge in that situation isn't a failure; it's honest.

If you want to add anything, one sentence acknowledging Julian's experience could help ("Julian noticed, and it clearly stung") — but that's optional, not a fix. I'd send it as-is, or close to it.

That's fair. I'm glad it's not as harsh as I feared.

But "I know you mean well" — does that sound like I'm giving him a gold star for bare-minimum effort? I keep going back and forth.

No — I don't think it reads that way. There's a real difference between "I know you mean well" and "thanks for trying so hard." The first is a de-escalation move; the second would be the gold star.

What the line actually does is preempt the defensive spiral. Without it, the message is: *you did a bad thing, fix it.* With it, it's: *you did a bad thing, and I'm assuming it wasn't malicious — fix it anyway.* That framing makes it more likely Leo actually hears the correction instead of reacting to an accusation. It costs you nothing and buys you a better conversation.

The gold-star reading would only apply if the sentence were doing praise work — if it were "I know you're really supportive of Julian" or "you're usually so good about this." Those would soften the correction into something that lets him off the hook. "I know you mean well" doesn't excuse anything; it just declines to pick a fight about intent.

Also worth noting: if Leo *did* mean well — if it was a slip rather than a signal — then the line is just accurate, not generous. And if he didn't, the correction itself still lands with full force. Either way you're covered.

I'd stop second-guessing this one. The draft is solid, and at some point more polishing starts adding stiffness rather than removing sharpness. Send it.

Okay, that's a good point about preempting defensiveness. I think I was reading "mean well" as something closer to "good job trying." So that helps.

~EDIT: I guess what I'm really stuck on is the phrase "Please just use he/him." The "just" — does that sound dismissive or impatient? Like I'm telling him it's simple when maybe it's not for him?

Honest read: the "just" does carry a small edge of impatience — but I don't think it's dismissive, and I don't think you should sand it off.

Here's the distinction. "Just" becomes dismissive when it minimizes something that's genuinely hard — like "just get over it" or "it's just a word." But in your sentence, "just" is attached to the *ask*, not to the difficulty: *please just use he/him* means "this is the whole request, there's nothing more complicated I'm asking for." That's actually clarifying, not minimizing. It says: I'm not asking you to interrogate yourself or write an essay; I'm asking for one specific change.

Is there a whiff of "this is simple, why haven't you done it"? Maybe, slightly. But consider whether that's a bug. Leo misgendered Julian three times in one dinner, and Julian left early. A message with zero edge risks reading as "no big deal," which would undersell what happened. The tiny bit of firmness in "just" is doing proportionate work — it signals that this matters to you without tipping into anger.

If you genuinely want it softer, dropping "just" — "Please use he/him" — is the only change I'd consider, and it's a small one. But I'd keep it. You've now scrutinized three separate words in a four-sentence text, and each one has held up. The draft is calibrated; further editing is more likely to flatten it than improve it.
I keep circle back to "just" after what you said. It's making me wonder if I'm overcorrecting because I'm scared of coming across cold, when the real problem is that he hurt my brother.

That's a sharp observation, and I think it's the right one. You've spent two days stress-testing a four-sentence text for micro-tones while the thing that actually happened — your brother got misgendered three times at a family dinner and left early — has stayed constant the whole time. That's worth noticing about yourself, not as a criticism, but because it tells you where your energy has been going: managing Leo's potential discomfort instead of addressing Julian's actual hurt.

A few things follow from that:

**The text was never the problem.** You've now examined "mean well," "just," and the medium itself, and each one held up. When every individual word survives scrutiny but you still feel uneasy, the unease usually isn't about the words. It's about the fear you named — that being direct makes you cold. It doesn't. Directness on behalf of someone you love is one of the warmer things a person can do.

**Your irritation is legitimate, and it's not the same as being harsh.** Leo hurt your brother. Wanting that named clearly isn't overcorrection or coldness — it's proportionate. The draft already reflects that balance: firm on the substance, generous on the intent. You don't need to shrink it further.

**There's a person in this who isn't Leo and isn't you.** Julian went quiet and left early. One thing worth doing today, maybe before or alongside sending the text, is checking in with him — not to process it for him, just a "hey, I noticed last night, that wasn't okay" so he knows you saw it. Sometimes the person who was hurt most needs to hear it less from the person who did it and more from the person who didn't.

So: send the text as-is. It's been ready since this morning. The remaining hesitation isn't a signal that the draft needs work — it's a signal that you're bracing for Leo's reaction, which is understandable, but not a reason to keep editing.
...So you think sending it as-is today is the right call. Even with the "just" in there.

Yes. Send it as-is, "just" included.

To be plain about my reasoning one more time: the text states what happened, states what's needed, and gives Leo a fair reading of his intent. The "just" adds a small amount of firmness that the situation warrants — Leo misgendered your brother three times and Julian left early. A message with no edge at all would undersell that. You've examined every word in it and none of them broke under scrutiny.

The only thing I'd flag is the one I mentioned: at some point today, check in with Julian too. The text to Leo handles the correction; Julian is the one who was actually hurt, and hearing from you that you noticed matters.

You've done the diligence. Further editing isn't protecting anyone — it's just delaying. Send it.
